summary: Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix one element at a time, like sorting playing cards in your hand: take the next card and slide it left into its place. It is fast on small or nearly sorted input.

sections.heading: Algorithm
bullets: Treat a[0] as a sorted prefix of length 1.
Take key = a[i] for i from 1 to n-1.
Shift every larger element in the prefix one slot right.
Drop the key into the gap.

sections.heading: Walkthrough
sections.body: On [5, 2, 4, 1]: key 2 shifts 5 giving [2, 5, 4, 1]; key 4 shifts 5 giving [2, 4, 5, 1]; key 1 shifts 5, 4, 2 giving [1, 2, 4, 5].

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Best (already sorted): O(n), one comparison per element.
Stable (stop shifting on equal values, i.e. use `>`).
Adaptive: runs in O(n + d) where d is the number of inversions.
Online: can sort elements as they arrive.

sections.heading: Why it matters in practice
sections.body: For small n the low overhead beats O(n log n) algorithms, so production sorts use it as a base case: Timsort and introsort switch to insertion sort on short runs (around 16-32 elements).
Find the insertion point with binary search in O(log i) comparisons, then shift. Comparisons drop to O(n log n), but shifting still costs O(n²) moves, so total time stays O(n²).

Run insertion sort on elements h apart for a decreasing sequence of h values, ending with h = 1. Far elements move quickly, and the final pass is nearly sorted. Typical running time is between O(n log² n) and O(n^1.5) depending on the gap sequence.
On a linked list the 'shift' becomes a pointer splice, so each insertion needs no moves, but locating the position is still a linear scan, keeping O(n²).

subtopics.title: Insertion vs bubble vs selection
subtopics.summary: How the three O(n²) sorts compare.

bullets: Insertion: best on nearly sorted data, stable, adaptive.
Bubble: stable and adaptive, but many more swaps.
Selection: fewest swaps, not adaptive, not stable.
